speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that I must again rise on a question of privilege. I do so with reference to a document that has come to all of us. It purports to be from my friend, Bruce Phillips, president of the National Press Club.
At the outset I should like to make it clear that all of us in this place know the difference between the National Press Club and the Parliamentary Press Gallery. As I say, this matter relates to the National Press Club which has its quarters in a government building located at 150 Wellington Street. This letter starts off as follows:
Honourable Members of the Senate and the House of Commons,
Gentlemen:
All of us received a copy of this letter. I checked with my friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis). She received it although it was just stuck in the box with no envelope. She does not know whether she is invited or not. She received the document but she is no gentleman. I understand the same dilemma obtains in respect of women members of the other place.
I know that in grammatical terms the masculine includes both masculine and feminine. I know that in the Interpretation Act the masculine is to be read both ways. But in the context of current events and in view of the fact that the National Press Club has in its constitution a ban on the admission of women to its membership and in view of the fact that this matter has been raised several times recently in Parliament, it seems to me this document is either an act of gross discourtesy to Members of Parliament, particularly the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and women members of the other place, or it is a calculated insult because of the questions we have raised about this matter.
The document is an invitation to all of us to attend an event which I should like to attend, for it has to do with recalling the anniversary of the night the House burned, but how can I? I point out that one reason for this question of privilege is that in the letter there is a specific request that the Speakers of both Houses and the leaders of all parties be in attendance. It seems to me that so long as the National Press Club practises discrimination we should consider seriously whether with propriety any of us, including Your Honour, can accept this invitation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to advise the House that most of the delays and difficulties which have recently been experienced in the government pay system have now been resolved.
In making this statement I would like to express my thanks to several hon. members who have brought particular pay problems and particular cases to our attention.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ISSUING OF RETROACTIVE PAY CHEQUES
speechtext: It is our pleasure.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ISSUING OF RETROACTIVE PAY CHEQUES
speechtext:
At this time I would like to report on the present position in the Central Pay Office and also on the government's plans for continuing to improve the pay process.
January 30, 1970
3018	COMMONS
Public Service Retroactive Pay Cheques
During the past year the government has signed 78 collective agreements covering 185,000 of its employees. In addition, the government has negotiated another 36 collective agreements for employees in Crown Corporations, boards and agencies. Most of these agreements include retroactive pay increases back as far as two years or more. This enormous volume of pay changes imposed an unprecedented burden on the departmental personnel officers and also on our paying offices. The size of this burden is made evident by the fact that during the last nine months of 1969 the Central Pay Office alone issued over 100,000 cheques for retroactive pay increases.
It should be emphasized that at no time did the government pay offices fail to process and to issue regular salary cheques on time. The delays which have been of concern to the government and understandably frustrating to some of its employees have been with respect to the delays in receiving increases in pay.
When the backlog of pay changes began to climb as a result of the increasing flow of collective agreements, a number of steps were taken. We employed 75 additional personnel, we worked an average of 3,000 hours a month overtime, and we strengthened the management of the paying offices.
The result of these actions was that by last November we were able to meet our initial objective of having the paying offices in a current position with respect to the implementation of collective agreements; that is to say, if some employees were not receiving on time retroactive pay increases due them under a collective agreement, the problem was not in the paying offices but in other areas of the pay process. Every effort has been made through the personnel offices of the departments and through the staff associations to identify such cases and to take immediate action.
As soon as we were up to date with the implementation of collective agreements we were able to turn our full attention to the processing of normal pay changes, that is, pay changes for employees who are promoted, who go on leave without pay, who retire, or who change their medical or other deductions. Every month our paying offices receive more than 75,000 pay changes of this type. The backlog of these normal pay changes had built up to a serious level, but I am pleased to be able to report to the House that it has been reduced steadily in recent weeks and
IMr. Richardson.]

that within the next few days the backlog will be down to a very small number of unresolved cases.
Now that the current difficulties have been overcome-I want to emphasize this-because of the hard work of many people in the departments and in the paying offices, we have an opportunity to undertake a fundamental examination of the pay system. To make the most of this opportunity, and to help make certain that the recent difficulties will not recur, I intend to engage a firm of Canadian management consultants to examine all aspects of the government's pay system.

My intention is that our pay system should be re-examined in terms of its responsiveness to the present system of collective bargaining in the Public Service, in terms of its relationship to over-all government personnel policy, and in terms of the ease with which an individual can understand how his salary cheque is calculated. It is my hope that representatives of the staff associations will be actively involved in this examination to express the point of view of their members.
I hope I have made it clear, Mr. Speaker, that we intend to do everything possible to ensure that the pay system measures up to the high standards of the government and to the understandably high expectations of its employees.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to note the minister now feels that the Central Pay Office is in a current position with respect to the implementation of collective agreements. I wonder whether the minister is referring to agreements affecting employees in the Ottawa area or across Canada, for I was informed this week that 13 employees in my constituency have been waiting since last May for both their retroactive pay and increases under a collective agreement and, unless they received them in the mail today, are still waiting to secure the increases agreed upon.
The minister points out the large volume of collective agreements and the tremendous volume of changes in the amount employees have received both in pay increases and retroactive pay, but there can be no excuse for the very substantial delays that have developed between the signing of agreements and the date on which such increases have
January 30, 1970

been effected. The government knew what would transpire when the system was altered but, like everything else this government does, they did not prepare themselves for the situation that did in fact develop and as a result people have suffered and continue to suffer.
Now the minister informs us that the future will be bright because another firm of management consultants will be hired by the government to examine all aspects of the government pay system. At this late date the minister has decided that the whole pay structure system should be examined. If the government continues to hire management consultants at the present rate we will soon be informed that they are hiring a firm of management consultants to study the work of the multitude of management consultant firms they have retained to study the oversights they have failed to anticipate when they undertook changes. If management consultants were required by the Department of Supply and Services, they were required before and not after they got into this mess, and surely they should be able to determine now within the government service, and without the additional expense of outside consultants, what should be done. The Department of Supply and Services should be setting an example for other departments in examining and solving problems rather than shifting the onus to agencies outside the government to solve problems that should not have been allowed to develop with such severity and dislocation in the first place.
The minister must know that his explanation is far from satisfactory with regard to the inability of his department to deal with the situation that developed. Certainly the 185,000 employees know this to be the case.
Because of the inability of the government to anticipate the problems that would ensue the taxpayers of this nation have been burdened with the expense of an additional 75 employees and payment for 3,000 hours of overtime. This, Mr. Speaker, is just not good enough and indicates the inability of this government to cope with the problems of the day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CANADA SHIPPING ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COST OF MEDICAL AND HOSPITAL SERVICES TO CREW
speechtext:
Bill C-10 deals, in the main, with amendments to the existing legislation provided in Part V of the Canada Shipping Act and includes an amendment to Part IV of the Canada Shipping Act.
The concept of a prepaid medical insurance and hospital insurance plan for ill or injured seafarers from vessels of foreign registry entering Canadian ports originated in the last century, in fact before Confederation, in the province of New Brunswick. The purpose of this plan was to set up a fund to defray the cost of medical and surgical treatment and hospitalization provided to a sick mariner and to prevent these costs becoming a charge on the community where such were incurred when the vessel set sail and left ill seamen behind.
At confederation, the responsibility for administration of this service was transferred to the federal government and was expanded to include other maritime provinces. This service was later extended, on an optional basis, to provide sick mariners benefits to crew members of Canadian registered fishing vessels. The fund to provide these services was accrued by the collection of dues, that is, a levy or a duty, calculated on the basis of the

tonnage of the vessel. Existing legislation provides for the collection of two cents per ton on the occasion of the first three entries in a Canadian port in the calendar year. It is obligatory for certain vessels, including foreign vessels, and optional to Canadian vessels engaged in the fishing industry.
Until the early 1940's, the revenues collected closely approximated the expenditures. During the 1940's costs spiralled; revenues remained fixed by statute and could not be adjusted to meet the increased costs. This disparity developed chiefly in respect of government vessels, fishing vessels of Canadian registry and vessels operating exclusively in Canadian waters. The government departments were requested to withdraw from the plan, which they did in 1956. In recent years, the revenue collected from foreign vessels has closely approximated the costs and, in fact, in some years has exceeded the expenditures. The over-all deficit incurred in operating the service has resulted from the provision of the services to crews of Canadian fishing vessels and vessels operating exclusively in Canadian waters.
Many changes in respect of medical care and hospital insurance have occurred since this legislation was enacted. A number of schemes for medical care insurance have been available to Canadians. With the advent of prepaid medical care insurance in some provinces, a considerable number of Canadian fishermen and mariners are adequately protected. In certain provinces, they may be protected by the provisions of the workmen's compensation board and in all provinces the provisions of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act are applicable.
Many changes in respect of the shipping industry have occurred as well. The small vessel with a large crew complement has been replaced by the large mechanized vessel with a small crew complement. In addition, medical care insurance plans are available to the owner of a vessel and many foreign shipping companies have taken advantage of these schemes to provide protection for their crews. As Canada is one of the few nations, if not the only nation, that provides sick mariners benefits, many shipping companies have appreciated the need to cover their crew with an insurance plan applicable in any port in the world. It is apparent that the obligation to pay dues in order to enter a Canadian port results in a duplication of these particular costs to the owner or agent of a foreign shipping company which, no doubt, contributes to increased transportation costs to Canadians.
January 30, 1970

The minister's decision to amend Part V of the Canada Shipping Act has followed deliberations within the department as a result of consultation with concerned colleagues in the Departments of Transport, Fisheries and Forestry, Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Manpower and Immigration and Justice.
The amendments presented as Bill C-10 effect repeal of the provision to collect dues and to provide medical treatment without charge to ill or injured crew members from vessels of foreign registry but retain, on an optional basis, provision for the collection of dues and medical care to ill or injured seamen from a Canadian vessel engaged in the fishing industry, providing these services are not available by reason of a federal-provincial cost sharing agreement under the Medical Care Act. The plan has never operated in either of the two northern territories nor in the inland waters of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta.
In the event a sick mariner from a foreign registered vessel is not covered by a medical care insurance plan, it is deemed necessary to amend Part IV of the act by the addition of a clause requiring ship owners to take responsibility for costs of health care to crews.
To summarize, we have legislation which was enacted, in the main, for two reasons. One of these reasons is now almost non-existent, the other is now thwarted. It is proposed to continue to provide medical care insurance but not hospitalization for crew members of Canadian fishing vessels, the masters of which elect to pay sick mariners dues before the first fishing voyage in the calendar year, in those provinces which do not have an operating medical care insurance scheme, provided Part V of the Canada Shipping Act formerly operated in that province. This results in the proposals of Bill C-10 operating in the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island, until such time as these provinces implement a medical care insurance program.

Again, we have a situation where the master of a ship must apply in writing. I expect there is a standard form for this. If I am wrong, I hope the parliamentary secretary will correct me, but it would seem to me that this provision would not apply in a province where there is a medical care plan. I also wonder whether the latter provision applies only to fishing vessels or whether it applies to other vessels as well. I have an interest in getting some information about the effect of the bill on those sections of the Canada Shipping Act which, to say the least, are obsolete and archaic and which raise all sorts of questions about the possibility of a continuing colonial status for Canada.
One question I have is whether this bill would apply as equally to denizens as it does to fishermen or seamen. I was rather struck by the oddness of that word and by the fact that apparently there is an opportunity for the government, exercising the royal prerogative I suppose, to grant to some people letters of denization. There is no other indication in the bill as to just what this means. How does one go about getting them? Are there any forms? Have such letters ever been issued? Are there any denizens in Canada?
The parliamentary secretary chuckles, and I do not blame him because this seems such a weird reference to have in the law of Canada. Yet there it is in the section of the Canada Shipping Act relating to the registering of ships. Apart from that section relating to the registering of ships, there is no reference to Canadian citizens. The only reference is to natural-born British subjects or persons recognized by law throughout Her Majesty's dominions as having the status of natural-born British subjects, who can register or own ships liable for registration within Canada. Also of course, the provision applies to persons who are made denizens by letters of denization.
I looked up the word in the dictionary, but even that did not help very much. I knew

January 30, 1970
Canada Shipping Act
that denizens were habitues of a certain area, for instance, we know that a rabbit is a denizen of the forest because he happens to live there, and there are denizens of the deep. These are supposed to be supernatural monsters of some sort and were described in imaginative terms in the early days of sailing ships. But to see this word in a statute of Canada does make valid the argument that the government is not really concerned about updating the laws of the nation but is engaged in a program of patching British law which existed before the turn of the century.
All we have done, Mr. Speaker, has been to carry that law forward, making some slight alterations as time went on but maintaining the basis of a document with colonial or imperialistic flavour. We have no Canada Shipping Act as such; it is subservient to British law.
Had the government really wanted to do something effective, it might have dealt with the Canada Shipping Act in total instead of only with a minor, insignificant part such as we are dealing with at the moment. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) has pointed out, this particular part is fraught with difficulty and misunderstanding. Members of the Official Opposition have indicated their doubts as to the real value of the bill itself.
If the government is only concerned with stacking-up a record of getting bills through Parliament, it could spend its whole time running insignificant pieces of legislation through the House and then point to a record of accomplishment in the passage of legislation. Of course, in reality it would not have accomplished much.
Referring to the Earl Jowitt dictionary of English law, I find the following definition of denizen:
A denizen in the primary but obsolete sense of the word is a natural-born subject of a country, or a native or inhabitant of a city or liberty.
Then, there is a quotation which reads:
If the King and his subjects should conquer another kingdom or dominion [they] are all citizens of the kingdom or dominion conquered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present to the House for its consideration Bill S-12 a new act to prevent the introduction into Canada of infectious or contagious diseases. The short title may be cited as the Quarantine Act. This bill was given first reading in the Senate on November 18, 1969. Two days later, debate on second reading commenced during which many informative and valuable remarks were made. After study before the Senate Health, Welfare and Science Committee, the committee report was presented on December 10, 1969 which contained a few amendments clarifying some questions that had been raised. The bill was then read a third time and passed on December 16, 1969.
The Quarantine Act is now contained in chapter 231 of the Revised Statutes of Canada and was first made the subject of Canadian

January 30, 1970
Quarantine Act
legislation in 1868. Except for two amendments made at the end of World War I, the legislation has remained the same in substance and in context since first enacted more than 100 years ago.
As was reasonable at the time of its enactment, and even at the time of the amendments in 1918 and 1919, the text of the act was considered adequate to deal with inward traffic by ship to Canada, the language of the act speaking throughout of "masters of vessels", of quarantine stations at maritime ports of entry, of coasting traffic and so forth. Nowhere does the act recognize by any reference the immense degree to which inward passenger and cargo traffic entails air travel, the use of numerous international airports or the frequency with which international air traffic must be received and admitted into Canada. Other developments and changes in the area of transportation and communications have similarly rendered obsolete certain other matters of substance, as well as the language of the Quarantine Act and, for this reason also, early revision is imperative. The urgency arises out of the degree to which the obsolescence referred to is increasing in significance and the difficulty of effecting useful quarantine measures becoming more marked.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
The quarantine service of Canada has a very interesting historical record which I will review only briefly. Attempts to control the introduction of communicable diseases by visiting travellers predates confederation and, indeed, most other forms of community public health services. The word "quarantine" dates back to the 14th century at least and is usually ascribed to the 40 days of isolation imposed by the local government on travellers arriving in certain Italian ports in an attempt to prevent them from infecting the local inhabitants. There were quarantine regulations in force at all major North American ports in colonial times. In Canada, the first Quarantine Act was passed by the first session of the first Dominion Parliament, and it was probably one of its first items of business. This act made the minister of agriculture responsible for administering the regulations. The first regulations made under the Canadian Quarantine Act were signed by the Governor in Council on May 23, 1868.
The original regulations make reference to only three quarantine stations located at Grosse Isle-an island in the St. Lawrence below Quebec city-at Halifax, and at Saint John, N.B. The stations at the latter two

points were situated at Lawlor's Island and Partridge Island respectively. All three stations predated confederation, having been established by the cities concerned in the early 1830's. The graves which may still be seen on these islands are mute evidence of the epidemics of smallpox, cholera and typhus which raged at that time. Additional stations were opened from time to time on the east coast as increased maritime traffic required, and in 1884 the first station was established on the west coast at Victoria, or more precisely at Albert Head and subsequently removed to William Head. By 1896, additional stations had been opened on the west coast and a medical superintendent of quarantine for British Columbia appointed.
During these early years cholera and typhus from Europe, yellow fever from South and Central America and the West Indies, cholera from the Far East, and smallpox from everywhere were the most feared. The last quarantine at Grosse Isle was in 1928-29 for smallpox; at Halifax in 1937-38 for smallpox, and in 1944-45 for typhus; at Saint John in 1920-21 for smallpox, and at William Head in 1938-39 for smallpox and in 1945-46 for typhus.
Quarantine stations at Grosse Isle, Halifax, Saint John and William Head, with their full facilities for large numbers of passengers, hospitals for treatment and large staffs with disinfecting equipment became unnecessary owing to the identification of the organisms of the diseases, methods of prevention by immunisation and vaccination, new medicines and treatments and improvement of world sanitation and international travel regulations. The quarantine station at Grosse Isle was closed in 1937, and subsequently the stations at Lawlor's and Partridge Islands were closed, and in 1959 William Head was closed. Canada now has five organized quarantine stations at Quebec, Halifax, Saint John, New Brunswick, St. John's, Newfoundland, and Victoria, B.C., with their substations. In addition, there are unorganized inland and maritime quarantine stations where customs officers act as quarantine officers.
The responsibility for the quarantine service was transferred from the department of agriculture to the department of immigration and colonization for one year, then to the department of health in 1919 which in 1928 became the department of pensions and national health. In 1944, responsibility was transferred to the Department of National Health and Welfare with the passing of the National Health and Welfare Act.
January 30, 1970

The general pattern of quarantine operations remained substantially the same until after World War II, although these decades were marked by a gradual diminution of the major quarantinable diseases. During the 1940's, increased attention was given to health problems on an international scale, and on October 1, 1952 the international sanitary regulations of the World Health Organization to which Canada subscribed without reservation from the outset, came into effect. Prior to World War II the quarantine service was concerned with marine traffic only. Commercial aircraft capable of carrying passengers to Canada from outside North America did not exist.
Soon after World War II the situation began to change rapidly and the establishment of quarantine offices at airports became necessary. In the succeeding two decades, the rate of growth of commercial aviation outstripped almost all other forms of transport, and now the number of persons arriving by air cleared through quarantine each year exceeds one million. The number continues to increase by about 15 per cent annually. This development has significantly changed the entire pattern of quarantine problems.
The reduction of quarantinable diseases throughout large areas of the world, as well as the greatly improved rapid methods of reporting incidence of disease which have been developed by the World Health Organization, have substantially reduced the danger of importation of major quarantinable disease by maritime traffic as infected areas are, for the most part, located sufficiently far away from Canada and it is impossible for vessels to complete the journey within the incubation period of the disease. Aircraft, however, readily transport passengers from highly infected areas to Canadian airports within a single day.
While vigilance must be maintained in respect of marine traffic and especially to guard against the importation of plague by rodents, air traffic has become of primary concern. This is further aggravated by the natural tendency of the passenger and the carrier not to lose the advantage of speed inherent in air travel by time consuming inspection procedures on arrival, and pressures for expeditious clearance of passengers continually increase. A new age is imminent. High capacity aircraft carrying up to 500 persons will begin operating this year. Supersonic aircraft capable of crossing the Atlantic in approximately three hours will be in opera-
Quarantine Act
tion later in the decade. Both will bring with them their particular problems.
Bill S-12, a recasting of the quarantine act, is designed to minimize the risk of importation into Canada of the major quarantinable diseases which, fortunately, have been eradicated in Canada but which, if imported, could be the cause of serious morbidity and, indeed, mortality. Our major concern is in respect of smallpox, cholera and plague, and this is reflected in the clauses of Bill S-12. We are aware of the improvement in global health conditions resulting from preventive health measures applied in other states which, in certain areas, were undertaken with the assistance of the World Health Organization. However, until the major quarantinable diseases are eradicated from the world, legislation which provides authority to inspect and examine international passengers and international carriers entering Canada for the purpose of determining the risk presented to public health, is necessary.

Obviously there was a need for amendment here, a need for change. The recent experience of passengers aboard the liner which was held up off the west coast is an indication of the difficult situations which can arise in the modern world and which give rise to a need for change. Quarantine Act
this chamber at the time this act was passed. This circumstance in itself is reason enough for considering changes in the regulations. It is likely that the bill will receive close examination in committee; there are many technical aspects involved which obviously are not susceptible of being dealt with adequately here.
There is one point I should like to make at this time. This bill, like so many others this session, provides that the usual wide discretionary powers be given to the Governor in Council to act by order in council, by regulation or by decree. I call this to the attention of the House as I have done in the case of so many bills in the past.
This morning I raised this particular issue by addressing questions to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in which I referred particularly to the report of the Special Committee on Statutory Instruments which goes right to the heart of the question raised by clause 19 of the bill before us. The very widest powers are given by that clause to the Governor in Council to enact various regulations, including the power to require persons arriving in Canada to produce to a quarantine officer evidence of immunization to any infectious or contagious disease.
There was an interesting discussion on this subject in the other place. One hon. Senator proposed there should be included in the regulatory power a right to provide for exemptions, and he gave certain reasons in support of his view that this power ought to be included. As I read from the proceedings of the Committee on Health, Welfare and Science in the other place, he suggested:
That persons with eczema or diseases such as leukemia, lymphoma, or generalized malignancy or those who may have lowered resistance such as from therapy with steroids, alkylating drugs, antimetabolites or radiation, or during pregnancy in which immunization is deemed to be contra-indicated, be exempted from this section at the discretion of the quarantine officer.
This was opposed by hon. Senators who were supporters of the government. I notice that one Senator from Calgary, speaking of the need for exemption in the case of a pregnant woman, asked: "How are we going to know whether a woman is pregnant or not when a lot of them do not know themselves?" I consider this to be a very weak answer to the suggestion made by the Senator who proposed the amendment. Nevertheless, it illustrates the point I tried to make this morning, one which was evaded by the Presi-

dent of the Privy Council and passed off by the Prime Minister in a rather humorous way.
If we give to this government or to any government the right to legislate by order in council, as we are being asked to do in clause 19, it is imperative that Parliament be provided with the means of checking these regulations.

Someone said: Let no man stand between me and my liberty. Well, day after day, year after year, we continue, while legislating on behalf of the people of Canada, to give away rights which are theirs and which they have given us no mandate to destroy as we are now doing. It is becoming an accepted fact that in any legislative program the first thing to be prepared is the section having to do with regulations; all the rest is then built around it. It is the case here. subtopic: PROVISION FOR RELIEF OF CONVICTED PERSONS
speechtext:
that Bill C-5, to provide for relief of persons who have been convicted of offences

January 30, 1970
Criminal Records
and subsequently rehabilitated themselves, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill represents an attempt on the part of the government to bring forward legislation that will deal with one aspect of the field of corrections that has been causing concern to all those working in the field and to public figures who have thought about the subject. The area I speak about is the apparently unjust consequences that still attach to a person who has been convicted of an offence but who has long since rehabilitated himself and become integrated into society in a wholly satisfactory way.
The consequences, in those circumstances, of having a conviction can work many injustices as well as leaving a stigma on the character of the person. This, it would seem clear, should be removed to the extent it is possible to do so. The great interest and concern in this subject was well evidenced by the private bill brought forward in the last Parliament in 1966 and dealt with in a committee of this House in the next year, as well as subsequent bills that have been brought forward in this Parliament.
The approach in this bill is quite different from that in the bill brought forward by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Tolmie). His private bill sought to deal with the matter differently; I think the term used was "expunging the records of the courts". This bill approaches the problem in a different way. It is an attempt to remove the consequences of the conviction and we believe will be more effective in achieving the desired objectives. The objectives, of course, in any of the legislation submitted for consideration by the House were never in question. It is a matter of working out the best method of achieving the objectives and, unfortunately, there is no background of statistics on this subject that is of much help. There is very little, other than the actual experience of the workers in this field.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The bill itself approaches the problem in this way: It provides that the person concerned make application and the National Parole Board, which we believe to be the body best equipped to examine into these kinds of problems and with the most experience in this field, examine into the particular case and make the recommendation for the grant of a pardon if the facts warrant it.

The grant of a pardon, in itself, does not necessarily solve all problems but it seems to be the closest approach we know towards solving some of the problems that arise in these cases. It will be seen when the bill is examined in committee that it provides for the procedures of the board and makes significant provisions relating to the grant of a pardon. Clause 5 of the bill reads as follows:
5. The grant of a pardon (a) is evidence of the fact that the Board, after making proper inquiries, was satisfied that an applicant was of good behaviour and that the conviction in respect of which the pardon is granted should no longer reflect adversely on his character; and (b) vacates the conviction in respect of which it is granted, unless the pardon is subsequently revoked.
Thus, the pardon is evidence of rehabilitation of good character and it vacates the conviction. It does these three things.
There is a subsequent provision in the bill that deals with the withdrawal of records. The approach to this aspect, which we believe to be the best approach we can work out, is the following: It is not accurate to say that a record that has been made many years ago can be physically obliterated, because there are records in the memories of other persons, there are newspaper reports and there is all sorts of documentation in many places. What we have sought to do here, and we think this will prevent the improper use of old records, is to have them withdrawn to the central authority in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police where they then can be sealed and only brought out under the limited conditions, set out in the act, when it is apparent that their use would be necessary. That is the approach to that problem.
As hon. members know, there has always been a right to grant a pardon under the royal prerogative of mercy. It is interesting to know that in the whole period of 40 years from 1910 to 1959 inclusive, there were only 32 ordinary pardons granted under the royal prerogative of mercy. Perhaps I should give some more recent figures. In 1966, the year the Department of the Solicitor General was created, 21 ordinary pardons were granted. In 1967, there were 36 ordinary pardons granted; in 1968, there were 75 ordinary pardons granted and in 1969, and I shall speak about the pardons of 1969 in a particular way in a moment, some 131 pardons were recommended by the National Parole Board under the existing procedure.
So, hon. members can see the increase in the use of this prerogative. That increase in use stems from the fact that, in an effort to
January 30, 1970

find some kind of solution or get started towards a solution to this problem, we began to use the royal prerogative of mercy as a method of granting pardons. This in large measure, although not quite, is what will be achieved under the legislation. By itself, the present procedure is rather cumbersome. Actually, until this bill is passed, there is only authority for the minister to request the parole board to look into each individual case and then, in each individual case, sign a recommendation to His Excellency, the Governor General and have the individual's pardon granted by His Excellency, the Governor General.
It will be seen that that procedure is not adequate at all to deal with the problem but it was very useful in giving the parole board and those authorities concerned in the field of correction a lot of administrative experience. In addition, the procedure helped in finding out what would best meet the problems that arise with those persons who have been unfortunate enough to have a conviction registered against them but have long since rehabilitated themselves and re-established themselves. This experience, which has been sharply accelerating throughout the latter part of the year, has indeed been very useful and has confirmed us in the belief that the approach evidenced in this bill is the best approach in trying to deal with the problem.
There will be, of course, sharply increased numbers of these applications once the bill is passed. The very limited experience so far indicates or appears to indicate that it would be very useful in meeting these problems. There is a lot of detail about the bill that can best be discussed in committee when the appropriate officers who deal with these problems are available. I, for one, welcome the opportunity to have the bill before committee so that all hon. members who are interested and concerned in this subject can ask the questions they wish, obtain all the information that is available and make suggestions that may be helpful in improving the bill.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
I for one do not view the bill as the final answer. I hope it will get quick passage through the House and then be re-examined at the end of two or three years experience when we will be in a better position to know what improvements can be made in the administrative procedure and what changes and other improvements should be made to its provisions.
Criminal Records
Already we have found, since embarking on this course, that we have been able to do a great many things of a beneficial nature, particularly in the employment field. This has been the result of co-operation on the part of personnel officers and management in a great many large firms. The response and attitude in that regard have been rather good. The available information in this regard can be given to hon. members at the committee stage. One of the things we had not anticipated, which seems to have been very effective, is that we grant a pardon as distinct from trying to deny that there ever was a record. That approach seems to have been very well received.
Already there have been changes made in what we might now regard as rather offensively worded questions on this subject which appear on many applications for employment. That whole aspect of the subject should be examined in committee. It is possible that we will require further legislation on that aspect after a review of the administrative practices and some experience with the measure. I hope we will not prematurely introduce compulsory legislation forcing people to do certain things, at least at this stage. As a result of our limited experience so far, I hope we do not make the granting of a pardon an automatic process. That does not seem to create a situation most beneficial to the one who has a record but has successfully rehabilitated himself.
I do not think there is much more 1 can usefully add on this subject. I welcome the opportunity of putting the bill before the House and I am sorry we were not able to put it forward earlier. I welcome the opportunity of discussing this matter with hon. members at the committee stage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was privileged to be a member of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs during the last Parliament. This committee spent part of two sessions on the subject of the destruction of criminal records, and it considered several private bills submitted by hon. members of this House. The evidence was not completed during the first session of the 27th Parliament and the meetings carried through into the second session. Finally, a report dated December 19, 1967, was made to the House.
In the first place, I commend the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) for making a move on this subject. There was a very great divergence of opinion in the committee as to how this matter should be approached. The committee was not prepared to make an absolute and final recommendation, although it did make a report. The report recommended that legislation be enacted incorporating the principle of expunging criminal records on the basis of several considerations. I do not want to read the five or six considerations in full, because obviously they have been considered by the Solicitor General who adopted a completely different approach from that recommended by the committee.
At this stage I think we should take a brief look at this principle before it goes to the committee for further consideration. A question just raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) concerning the effect a pardon would have on a person who has been convicted of one criminal offence, with no further record for a period of five years, who had led a normal and reformed life and then applies for one of the special things for which many people apply. The individual

may apply for an immigration visa to go to another country, either for a short term or to work; he may apply for a bond in connection with employment he is about to take; he may apply for employment in an agency which requires a form to be filled out.
One question almost always asked on these forms is: Have you ever been convicted of a criminal offence? The wording of the bill as presented is a little vague. I should like to ask the Solicitor General, a couple of questions if I can get his attention, which perhaps he will answer when closing the debate.
The first question relates to the type of question already asked. Clause 5(a), which is the effective clause, says that the granting of a pardon vacates the conviction in respect of which it is granted. The word "vacates" is one I cannot recall having been used in legal terminology except in respect of certain actions which have been taken in the courts. Does the Solicitor General feel that if a pardon vacates the conviction, the person involved is entitled to say, "I do not have a criminal record" or, "I have not been convicted"? If the conviction is vacated, what does it mean? It certainly does not go as far as the meaning of the word "expunge," which is the word that kept coming up during the discussions in the committee.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I believe we are left pretty much in the dark in respect of the real effect of this legislation. If the granting of a pardon vacates a conviction, may we assume that the conviction has been wiped out? A question was asked of the minister concerning the forms being changed so that the question would be: Have you ever been convicted of an offence for which a pardon was not granted? If a provision were included in the legislation to require application forms to contain a question of this type, I think 99 out of every 100 doubts members of the committee had would be answered.
I hope the minister will say that in respect of a criminal offence for which a person could be subsequently pardoned, nobody may include in an application form of any kind a question other than the one set out in the act. I believe this is the meat of the whole problem. Such a clause, however, is not in the bill. I do not know whether it was considered and abandoned, or whether it was not considered.

The minister advises that it was considered, so presumably it was abandoned. I would like this matter to be reconsidered, because I think such a provision would eliminate the concern of many people. What is the use of having a procedure whereby a conviction is wiped out and it is established that a person is of good character, if that person then became involved in filling out a form which asked if he was ever convicted of a criminal offence, to which he would have to answer "Yes"? This person would then find himself in further difficulties. However, if the question, "Have you ever been convicted of a criminal offence for which you have not been granted a pardon" were asked, he could answer "No" and that would be the end of the matter. I firmly believe the committee should take a very serious look at this matter when the bill comes before the committee. This is a point that everyone is concerned about.
A second point I should like to raise concerns offences for which a person was convicted in the past maybe once or maybe twice, which now have been made legal. Recently amendments to the Criminal Code were passed. I know of a number of cases in the past involving doctors who were convicted of performing abortions. I thought the convictions, as a matter of humanity, were outrageous. I agreed with some portions of the Criminal code bill, because many of these doctors were performing a service to humanity which if performed now would not involve a criminal offence.
The same argument applies to certain sexual offences which were under the Criminal Code. They were illegal one day, and on the following day they were legal. Should not a pardon be issued as a matter of course in such situations? I suggest this is another matter which the committee should examine, because in these cases the law has changed and such a person would not now be regarded as having a criminal record.
The third matter which concerns me a little is that of the one-time offender convicted some years ago perhaps of a minor offence; then years go by and he never applies for a pardon, perhaps on the ground that he does not think there is any record of the conviction or because he thinks this bill would wipe it out after five years. This is one of the dangers which arises in connection with the bill. Such a person may not apply for a pardon because he might think that because there was only one conviction of a minor

nature, all he would do by applying for a pardon would be to stir up things again. This would mean that the Parole Board would have to institute an investigation, and he would fear its officers visiting his home or people inquiring whether he was still, as the act states, a person of good character.
There may be many situations in which the person whom we are really trying to protect would be discriminated against because he made such application, whereas a person who did not would not be in the same position. It might sound as if I am splitting hairs, but I do not think I am.
A number of these people probably would be very hesitant about applying for a pardon because they might think they would rather let sleeping dogs lie until the day they have a chance to obtain a better job, move to another country or provide a bond for a friend. When this day comes, they suddenly find that the record which they thought was long dead is still there. As the minister has admitted, this bill does not cover such a situation.
Also, this bill does not cover the situation in respect of the record of juveniles. A lot of time was spent on this matter during the sittings of the standing committee. I have very strong views in respect of the records of juvenile offenders. According to the Juvenile Delinquents Act, these records are not to be used. A person under age 16 in Ontario, and under age 18 in some other provinces, is deemed not to be a criminal but rather a person in need of aid and assistance. The Juvenile Delinquents Act is so framed that such a person does not have a criminal record. But the police consider that there is a criminal record in respect of such a person.
The records in some juvenille courts are made available, improperly, to the police. I think that in respect of the very few cases where there is no further record of the offence, the record in the juvenile court should die there. I believe this bill should contain a clause amending the Juvenile Delinquents Act which would make specifically clear that all records of juvenile delinquents, after these persons have reached age 16, should be expunged, sealed and not reopened. One cannot say they were never there, but one can say they will never be referred to.

A person convicted of a criminal offence may answer "No" to the question on the application form. But there is much misuse of

Many bills that we pass in this House contain clauses amending acts, to make them conform. I would like the juvenile delinquents problem cleared up once and for all. I am glad to hear the minister say that he is considering some amendments to the act, and if he will bring in a bill shortly I will go on to another subject. There is no reason why, when we are dealing with expunging the record or getting rid of the record of past convictions, we should not touch on that subject.
This bill does not make any provision in regard to juvenile delinquents. I think that is a very serious shortcoming because so long as this situation continues the police and agencies connected with them will continue to consider juvenile delinquency records as relating to criminal offences, and this is not right. I make no exception even for a person who gets into trouble later in life; in these cases their past record should also be wiped out.
There is one other point I would like to make. It was stated during the hearings of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs that the police in fact have two records; the official record which we are trying to expunge- or vacate, in the wording of the bill-and an unofficial record which is sometimes called a police blotter type of record, which they keep separately.
This evidence was given by Chief Mackey, chief of the Toronto police, as recorded at page 59 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the committee meeting of November 2, 1967. Chief Mackey said very clearly that these records are all in special files, not in the ordinary police files, so the

argument of the police that they need them to catch up with known criminals is a fallacy. They do not need them, because they have the record in another file-a record which will never be expunged. In fact, there is no suggestion that police records will ever be expunged. They have their modus operandi files from which they catch up with people. They also have them in respect of juveniles.
We can never get rid of these records, and perhaps we should not. However, these records are not the ones I am talking about. I am referring to the public records which I believe should be dealt with in such a way that a one-time offender is assured that after a reasonable period of time someone will not come along and blackmail him because at one time he committed an offence about which no one has ever heard.
I would like to make one more point regarding the revocation of a pardon. Clause 7 provides that if it is established to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council that the person to whom a pardon was granted is no longer of good character, his pardon may be revoked. I think this is one of the most difficult clauses to accept. What is a person of good character, and who is to decide about it? We have always held that a person is innocent until proven guilty. In this country we do not draw a distinction between good people and bad people. They are all people, but they may have been convicted of an offence. Whether they are of good character is a matter of opinion in every case.
I think it will be very difficult to establish that a person is no longer of good character. If it were the other way round, I might not be so concerned. In other words, if the bill provided that a pardon would not be granted if a person was not of good character, perhaps there would be some argument for it. In that case it could be established to the satisfaction of the Parole Board that, in addition to being convicted of an offence, the person in question consorted with other persons who had been convicted and had engaged in activities that verge on criminal. Perhaps such a person had been found in the company of persons whose backgrounds made it obvious that he was leading a life of crime.
However, this clause is different-it relates to the revocation of a pardon. The man has been pardoned and his offence has been expunged from the record, then someone says that he is not of good character any more and his pardon will be revoked. This is a danger-
January 30, 1970

ous clause, because under these provisions a man can be convicted without trial, which is contrary to our understanding of the law.
I find acceptable that part of the clause which provides that if a person has made deceptive statements in his application, his pardon can be revoked. There is a perfectly valid ground for revoking his pardon if he has made incorrect statements, failed to disclose evidence, or information comes to light that was not revealed previously. However, the fact that a person is no longer of good character is, in my opinion, not sufficient ground for revoking his pardon.
I think that the principle of granting a pardon will be acceptable provided there are enough applications. There must be thousands and thousands of people in this country in the category of those whom this legislation is trying to help, and in favour of whom the committee made recommendations. How many of these people will apply for a pardon? If the number is small, the legislation will be a failure because it will not be achieving the effect that is desired.
I was glad to hear the minister say that the matter will be reviewed, because the number of convictions and pardons will eventually reveal the effectiveness of the statute. I agree that we must take some action. I would like these few matters to be reconsidered in the committee; therefore, I support the recommendation that the bill be referred to the committee. I hope the minister will be prepared to reconsider some of these points which do not go against the principle of the bill but which, if accepted, will make the legislation much more effective.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I should like to pay tribute to my hon. friend from Vancouver-East (Mr. Winch) for the interest he has shown throughout his life in penology and matters such as this. His activities in this connection began long before most hon. members took their seats in Parliament.
As Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition in the British Columbia legislature in the forties, he pioneered in an area which was delicate and not very acceptable socially, as did his father. I refer to institutions for mental care, penitentiaries, provincial jails and the like. He took an active interest in problems of rehabilitation, recidivism, parole and related questions. As I say, my hon. friend has shown a lifelong interest in such
Criminal Records
matters, and having known him personally for some time, I think he deserves commendation on this occasion.
While I am sure the bill is acceptable to everyone in a general sense, it is really not a pace-setter. If anything, it is a bit behind the public conscience in these matters. For some time now the ice has been broken in terms of greater industrial and social acceptance of persons who have been convicted of criminal offences. In addition, we know that the Department of the Solicitor General, through the Parole Board service, has been operating in this field, developing a certain expertise and sophistication in its approach to persons convicted of criminal offences, the expunging of records and the process of pardon which is being used.
I notice that the bill is all-inclusive. It refers to persons who might have been convicted under the Criminal Code or any other federal statute, but the wording in clause 3 indicates that application might be made by a corporate structure as well. In this regard we are aware that a number of companies and corporations in Canada have been convicted of criminal offences, of criminal conspiracy, and have been sentenced in the courts and fined under the Combines Investigation Act.
Technically speaking, these organizations, these companies, would be eligible to make application for pardon. Even the Electric Reduction Company, which we have heard mentioned recently, would be able to apply for a pardon and, presumably, receive one if it applied five years from the time it was convicted of contravening the criminal law of Canada. The difficulty is that there is an element of friendliness involved in the structure of a company, because it is not a company itself which engages in these criminal activities; it is the officials of the company. It is not the Electric Reduction Company which was guilty of criminal offences; it is people like Dr. Solandt who engaged in criminal activity. But he will not have to worry about applying for a pardon. In fact, he has already received one inasmuch as he is being maintained as chairman of the Science Council of Canada, and an endorsement of that kind precludes the necessity of involving himself in the procedure of applying for a pardon.
We are really dealing with persons-with human beings who have fallen foul of the law-and we Eire hoping to establish machinery sanctioned by legislation which will give them an opportunity to apply for the removal of the stigma attached to the commission of a

January 30, 1970
Criminal Records
criminal offence. The idea is that persons will apply, and thus set the process in motion. An investigation will be carried out by officers of the National Parole Board, as is done in practice at the present time.
I suggest that under the provisions of clause 4 there are two items which have been omitted. One concerns persons who are sentenced or dealt with under the Juvenile Delinquents Act. This aspect has been eloquently discussed by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) and does not need further elaboration.
The other omission relates to suspended sentences. The board can cause inquiries to be made when five years has elapsed since a sentence of imprisonment has been served, a period of probation ended or a fine paid. But in the case of a person who received a suspended sentence-and such sentences are often passed when young people are concerned, though not exclusively-I believe we are bound to recognize an area of omission.
In some ways a person who receives a suspended sentence finds himself in a situation which can last forever.' Presumably; at any time in the future a court could impose two sentences, should a further offence be committed-one for the current offence and one in respect of the original offence. It seems to me there should be some mechanism by means of which a suspended sentence could be regarded as though it had been imposed and served at the time of conviction. An opportunity should be provided for an individual in those circumstances to apply for removal of the right to impose a sentence after a period of time.
What concerns us in large measure is that an individual affected shall have the right or the opportunity to obtain gainful employment. There is an added psychological element involved-the relief which enters into the person's mind, the sense of well-being he experiences on receiving a pardon. In the few cases known to me in which individuals have applied for and received pardons under the procedure which exists at the present time, this sense of relief was present, as if a shadow had been wiped out and was no longer there to haunt the memory.
The federal government undertook a while ago to remove from all its application forms in connection with employment the question relating to criminal offences. I do not know whether Canadian National Railways still has a question of this kind on its application forms, but it did until not long ago. I know

there are individuals working for the CNR, as well as persons in the government service, who lied when they answered that because they wished to obtain employment and thought that if they answered the question honestly and admitted a criminal record, they probably would not obtain work. They are still employed. In some cases the employer knows about the misinformation which was supplied but has decided against taking any action; he has wiped it out and has not taken it as a reason for discontinuing the fellow's employment, which is a helpful and enlightened approach.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
In some types of employment there is not any great concern on the part of the employer whether the fellow has a criminal record or not. I worked as a logger on the west coast at one time. The primary desire of logging companies is to get production going, get the logs in the water and on their way to the mills. They do not really care whether a chap has a criminal record as long as he puts in a day's work and keeps up production.
However, companies involved in handling money and valuables are quite concerned about a criminal record, not so much because of the record itself but because it will probably prohibit bonding. This is an area that the government should become involved in; it should establish a substitute bonding arrangement. This is a kind of extension of the concept, but a logical one, and I think the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) feels as strongly about it as anybody.
Perhaps it is not possible to set up this mechanism for bonding through the federal government, but at least we can explore the possibilities in committee and maybe use this bill as a prelude to some other legislative arrangement. In this way individuals who fall into difficulty about bonding would be helped to find meaningful employment in fields which would otherwise be closed to them.
I think there is a failure in the bill with respect to the question that might be asked by prospective employers about a criminal record. This has already been touched upon by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka and by the minister. Whilst on the subject, I would say that I do not agree with the proposition made a couple of years ago that we change history by expunging criminal records-in effect saying that an individual did not commit a criminal offence.
January 30, 1970

I submit, even though it is argued by the other side that this is not the case, that although a person may receive a pardon, under this legislation a prospective employer would still be in a position to ask the simple question: Have you ever been convicted of a criminal offence? If the individual is honest about it, regardless of having received a pardon he would be required in conscience to answer that he had. I think we must follow the suggestion of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka and confine the type of question on applications for employment to simply: Have you ever been convicted of a criminal offence for which a pardon under the criminal records act has not been received? The individual would then, in all honesty, be able to answer "No" and that would prevent any further exploration.
According to our rules, Mr. Speaker, we cannot engage in a detailed discussion of clauses of the bill, but I hope I may be permitted to say a word or two on clause 6(2). This clause speaks of keeping records of people who have received a pardon, in the hands of the RCMP in a separate, locked vault. It also states that the existence of the record or the fact of the conviction shall not be disclosed to any person. I think the fact that in clause 6(2) there is reference to the conviction and the existence of a criminal record indicates that in fact the record still exists, in fact the conviction was imposed, in fact history has not been rewritten, and that though the individual may have received a pardon, he was convicted of a criminal offence. No matter what anybody says, always he will have been convicted of a criminal offence. He may have received a pardon, but he still was convicted.
History cannot be rewritten. Newspapers still exist, memories still exist, and as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka said, police forces still have memories. Detectives know which persons have records, and keep an eye on them. Even now, if an individual should receive parole the knowledge of the criminal background is available to the RCMP in his community. I know of two or three instances where individuals have in effect been hounded-not in the direct sense of being awakened every morning at four o'clock, but hounded by being watched and questions being asked about them. S'o memory exists in the police force and cannot possibly be wiped out.
Primarily, however, we are talking about employment. I think we can avoid an employer asking questions in a way that would elicit
Criminal Records
the information that a prospective employee had been convicted of a criminal offence, whether or not he had received a pardon. The bill provides that five years must elapse upon the completion of sentence, probation or payment of a fine, before the individual can apply for and receive a pardon. This leaves open to speculation and comment the period of time between his release from jail and the end of the five-year period. It is difficult enough for anybody to make a go of it upon release from jail at the completion of a sentence, but when employment opportunities are not as good all across the nation as at other times, it is even more difficult.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
For the sake of argument, a person released from jail at this time of year and at this point in our history would have more difficulty finding employment than if released during a period of high employment. Also, after two years in jail unemployment insurance benefits are not carried forward, so there is not that assistance to fall back upon. Many people have difficulty obtaining social welfare assistance and, surprisingly enough, many exconvicts have an element of pride which precludes them from applying for such assistance. Things are even more difficult, of course, in the absence of any real rehabilitation program. Although we talk about it a good deal, there is no rehabilitation program within our prison structure. Lip service is paid to the concept within our penitentiaries, but primarily our penitentiaries are places where you keep people locked up. That is their primary function and every person in authority, from the warden down to the most recently employed guard, thinks: We are here to keep the prisoners locked up, and maintain discipline. Clearly, those who are looking for any rehabilitative activity within our prison structure are butting their heads against a stone wall.
When a person receives parole there may be some hope for him, especially if he is able to obtain employment and if there are friends or individuals outside to assist him in getting off on the right foot. Where there is no such help, where there is no after care so to speak, the outlook for a former prisoner is not promising. The more people in our penitentiary structure look at a man as being a hardened criminal, the greater will be his difficulty in rehabilitating himself, no matter how much he should want that.
If 1 might inject my own thoughts here, it might be helpful if, for political reasons only,

January 30, 1970
Criminal Records
candidates of political parties in elections were to visit penitentiaries. It would be helpful if we gave the inmates of penitentiaries the right to vote in federal elections, because then candidates and members of political parties would pay more than lip service to the idea of rehabilitating prisoners. I am an advocate of giving the inmates of penitentiaries the vote. After all, the federal Parliament deals with their affairs after they have been incarcerated, but they have no real opportunity to communicate with us in this House. Because they do not vote there is no pressure on political parties to consider them, whereas there would be that pressure if inmates had the right to vote.
I have grave reservations about certain parts of clause 7 which relates to the revocation of pardons. If the Parole Board which granted the original pardon feels the individual is no longer of good character, or if the minister finds he is no longer of good character-no matter what that phrase may mean-the man's pardon may be revoked. I think the pertinent words in the clause are far too vague and too difficult to interpret and should not be retained in the legislation. Perhaps they will be removed in committee, or we might substitute other words for them. In any event, I think we should explore the ideas that would govern the revocation of a pardon or the not granting of an application in the first place.
Also, there appears to be no opportunity to appeal the rejection of an application. There is no opportunity to appeal the revocation of a pardon. Here we are granting by legislation a right that individuals enjoy under our common law; we are spelling it out and adding some characteristics that will give it force and effect. Along with our common rights there is a companion right which says that individuals shall be able to appeal to a court of last resort; yet in the construction of this bill it seems that there is no such right. It is true that the man makes his application to a certain authority; someone within the Parole Board will examine that application, will check with the RCMP or the city police, with former employers and the like, and may come to the conclusion that the person should not be granted a pardon. That, then, is the end of it.
It is true that the individual whose application has been rejected may go to the minister and, for argument's sake, say, "I have applied for a pardon and have not received it. Why not?" The minister will not conduct an inqui-

ry himself; instead, he will go back to the Parole Board, back to the same people who conducted the investigation in the first instance, and will receive from that body the grounds and premises upon which the original application was rejected. Since the minister will have no other information, he will have to advise the individual that this is all the information he has, and that will be the end of the matter.
Although the individual may have a right under law to appeal, that right is abrogated because in effect he will be appealing to that group which made the decision in the first place. I think this is not correct and that some counterbalancing factor ought to be introduced. I am sure the minister thought about this matter when preparing the legislation. Perhaps he will explore it further when we get into committee.
There is in society, as I said a while ago, a much stronger desire now to help those who have been convicted of criminal offences. If we could entice prospective employers, say to work directly with individuals who are inmates of penitentiaries and employ them, there is hope of rehabilitating those men who are lucky enough to be so employed. I do not think we should wait until a man gets out of jail and onto the street and then becomes involved in more trouble.
I have almost concluded my remarks, Mr. Speaker; it is almost four o'clock. If there is disposition on the part of hon. members to continue with the bill and proceed to its conclusion today, we will have no objection.
