speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the introduction of this bill by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) gives us today the opportunity to discuss a matter of utmost interest to almost all hon. members. It will soon become topic no. 1 because a forthcoming census will give rise to another revision of the electoral boundaries. Thus the debate might be useful on many counts.
I know that all hon. members recognize that all constituencies are to be established in the most logical, fair and equitable manner possible. Boundaries of electoral districts should be determined in such a way as not to leave too much margin, as it should not be harder or more difficult to represent one district rather than another. That situation, unfortunately, still prevails.
On this point, I share many of the views of the hon. member for Edmonton West, sponsor of the bill. As he aptly stated, the first revision, according to the bill adopted in 1964, was not a success, particularly in some of the provinces. The criteria described in section 13 of the act could perhaps be improved upon or altered to good purpose.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
But that was the first time we were using that procedure the purpose of which is to bring about viable political units, taking into account not only population but other criteria as well. To be objective, however, we must admit that it was not an easy task to divide the electoral map because of the vastness of the land, its other geographic characteristics and the number of sparsely populated areas.
DEBATES	3055
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act
Of course, as was said by the hon. member, this was a marked improvement on the old system. Previously, when a committee of the House met to redistribute the electoral map, members were often influenced by partisan considerations, which led to some illogical boundaries.
And it is quite to the honour of the 1964 Liberal government, under the right hon. Mr. Pearson, to have made adopted the principle of an impartial and independent commission to deal with this important but delicate task of reviewing periodicaly the riding limits. This action had generally been well received since it was a significant improvement on the previous system.
However, the Electoral Boundaries Commission had, in its decisions, to take into account the provisions of the act and particularly the principle under which the division of a province into ridings should be effected on the basis of population, keeping as nearly as possible to the electoral quota for the province, that is the quotient obtained by dividing the total population as ascertained by the census by the number of the House of Commons assigned to the province as calculated by the Representation Commissioner under section 12 of the act, subject and according with section 51 of the British North America Act and rules provided therein.
Now, it is to comply with the provisions of this legislation that chapter 31 of the 19641965 Statutes of Canada was drafted; in particular, section 13(c) stipulates that the Commission may depart from the rule I just mentioned, for geographic considerations or because of the diversity of interests of the inhabitants of various regions of the province, but the departure from the electoral quota for that province shall not exceed 25 per cent more or 25 per cent less.
Now, I think that at the time of the last redistribution, this exception provision was not used as often as it should have been or as it could be used. In most cases, this difference should have, at least, been taken into account, especially in rural ridings, which sometimes cover such a large area that it is virtually impossible for members to visit them as often as they wish and to get in touch with all their constituents.
I suggest that it is not the same thing to represent a rural district, which may include 50 or 75 rural, semi-urban or urban municipalities, with all the problems that this may imply, and to represent an urban dis-
January 30, 1970
3056	COMMONS DEBATES
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act trict, generally including a large community and sometimes being part of a large urban centre.
In such a case, this 25 per cent margin should have been fully allowed and this, I suggest, was not done at the last census. It might be advisable to amend these sections in order to give more discretionary power to the Commissioner and to take into account not only the population required to justify the establishment of an electoral district, but also the various demographic, geographic and economic factors.
Under the legislation, before drawing up its report, the Commission must hold public hearings in each province, following the publication of a preliminary report and of a map showing the proposed boundaries. During those hearings, any interested individual who has given notice within the required time can make some comments and suggest some changes.
Now, experience has shown rather clearly, I think, that once the map has been drawn up by the Commission, it is not easy to have it altered, to any great extent, because those changes would affect many neighbouring constituencies and as a result, the electoral map would become useless.
That is why, in my opinion, there have been so few changes, following the public hearings of 1965 or even following the subsequent debates in the House of Commons. In fact, the municipalities, the Chambers of Commerce and the intermediate bodies which submitted briefs often at great cost found that out the hard way. I was told many times that petitioners were not always welcomed by the Commission, even when, as was often the case, briefs revealed the existence of disparities or the inopportunity of combining some areas.
That is why it is most important, first of all, to make good appointments, to choose competent commissioners. However, we must not exclude necessarily those who were active in politics or choose only among judges or university professors as is often the case.
Commissioners have to be not only qualified but impartial also.
It has previously been said that they could be influenced by party considerations. I question that. It certainly did not happen during the latest census, at least not in the province of Quebec. Quite the contrary. As for me, the constituency I had been representing since 1963, that of Stanstead, disappeared. Follow-

ing the electoral redistribution, it was divided in three. I represent Magog where I live. This region was added to the provincial counties of Brome, Missisquoi and Iberville. As for the town of Iberville it became the new federal constituency of Missisquoi.
I can say that electors from the new regions which were added to the former Brome-Mis-sisquoi constituency were quite astonished, especially those residing in the provincial county of Iberville. In fact, following the annexation which followed redistribution, part of the town of Iberville and all the adjoining rural district became the Missisquoi constituency, whereas the remaining part of the town was included in the Saint-Jean constituency.
This is only one instance. The situation should be remedied on the occasion of the next electoral boundaries readjustment. However, I got over the whole thing by getting elected in a new constituency. There, I met active, hard-working and thoroughly Canadian-minded people. In that area, Englishspeaking and French-speaking people work together in harmony to build a better future.
The report of the Commission was finally tabled in the House. The purpose of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Edmonton West is to require the Commission to support with reasons the proposed changes.
As far as I am concerned, I have no objection to the commissioners explaining the changes they propose to make concerning the boundaries, the description or the name of the electoral districts. That might help Canadians to understand some decisions. Perhaps, they would not have had such an easy time of it on the last occasion. As a matter of fact, I had the impression they were concerned only with demography when the time came for redistribution.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
But, as indicated by other members in the debate of November 1968, especially by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner), I believe that the publication of the reasons might initiate a debate which, far from being shortened, could drag on considerably. In fact all hon. members are more or less dissatisfied and they would like to discuss the reasons given by the commissioners, because as they know their ridings they are probably very sensitive to that question.
January 30, 1970	COMMONS
I am afraid that this would give rise to lengthy debates with no practical results, because, as pointed out by the hon. member, the House cannot bring in any amendments. To do so, indeed, it is necessary that in the length of time prescribed by the Standing Orders, ten members should register an objection of which they ought to inform the Commission through Hansard or Votes and Proceedings. The Commission is supposed to study it in order to determine the motives advocated by the members.
Generally speaking, the members who know their area better than anybody and who, most of the time, have had talks with the people concerned, are those who can most likely make useful recommendations, without necessarily knowing what motivated the decisions of the commissioners.
I think that nothing prevents hon. members or anyone else from filing an objection with the Commission, or even previously with the Representation Commissioner, preferably before the preliminary report is tabled. It might then be for the members and other people concerned the ideal time to comment on it and to draw the attention of the Commission and of the Representation Commissioner to the blatant cases of discrimination.
Mr. Speaker, it might be advisable under the circumstances to amend the act, particularly Section 13. It is extremely important to appoint to these commissions people who have practical experience and who can draw from this experience in order to arrive at a fair delimitation of electoral constituencies, while keeping in mind the obvious difficulties which the commissioners must face.
I hope that the next revision will be a great improvement on the last one and that we will at least try to reach this aim as is no doubt the wish of all hon. members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am interested in the bill brought before the House by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). I express sympathy with the hon. member in connection with the problems he has raised for discussion and consideration.
I am aware that he and other hon. members, together with various interested people in Alberta, experienced difficulties in the most recent redistribution of boundaries because of the terms of the legislation. I have had some contact with the operation of this legislation, although I was not a member of the House
DEBATES	3057
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act when the act was debated in this chamber or when subsequent discussions took place regarding the decisions of the provincial boundary commissions. I was involved to the extent that I took part in making recommendations to the commission in my province of Saskatchewan, in my capacity as research director for the leader of the opposition in that province. I also went with him to present a brief to the commission on behalf of the New Democratic Party of Saskatchewan.
When the original legislation was passed by the House there was a fairly general feeling that hon. members wanted to do away with what had been termed gerrymandering, or the suspicion of gerrymandering. They wanted to do away with the decennial haggling which had taken place with regard to electoral boundaries. In effect, they wanted to take politics out of the process of drawing up electoral boundaries. This was very commendable and to this extent the act has represented a step forward.
Having the benefit of hindsight, however, I suggest that we lost sight of the fact that constituency boundaries are an essential feature of the political process. They cannot be separated from the political process or considered in some apolitical fashion completely apart from it. This was demonstrated when some of the shortcomings of the original act were recognized-when an amendment was introduced which at least provided for debate on the boundaries proposed by the commissions.
This amendment gave the provincial commissions an opportunity to review their proposals, taking into account objections which had been raised in the House of Commons. Final power still rested with the commissions, which were not required to give any reasons or set forth any rationale in support of their decisions.
There was considerable lack of response to some extremely valid points which were made in debate in the House of Commons at that time in objecting to proposals made by the commissions across Canada. Particular objections were raised with respect to the reports of the commissions in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia.
In some parts of Canada the reports of the commissions were sound and there was little objection to them. But in the three western provinces there were some very real difficulties. I do not think I need remind hon. members of the ghastly mistakes associated with boundaries in Alberta. There was also consid-
3058	COMMONS DEBATES	January 30, 1970
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act erable objection to boundaries in British Columbia. But after strong representations had been made, I believe only one change was brought about, and that was to boundaries affecting the Queen Charlotte Islands. In Saskatchewan, as in Alberta, no change was made in any of the boundaries, in spite of the very reasonable representations which had been put forward though the changes called for could have been implemented without any great difficulty.
I think it became clear during the course of the hearings that the initial report provided by the provincial commissions served as a basis for the final report, and that despite the soundness of any objections made to the commissions' proposals there was little chance of any change being made to the initial plan.
With respect to the commission operating in my own province of Saskatchewan, I wish to make it clear that I have the highest respect for the integrity of its members. It consisted of a well-known political scientist from the University of Saskatchewan, the Clerk of the Legislative Assembly of the province of Saskatchewan and a well-known judge on the bench of that province. In my view these gentlemen gave earnest consideration to the representations which were made. Nevertheless, it seems to me their immediate reaction to a representation was to say, "Well, the trouble is this-" and from there on they would proceed to defend the original proposals they had made public.
It was difficult to get anything by way of a sympathetic response. There was no effective communication between the commission and those who were interested in the boundaries it was establishing. There is no question about the apolitical nature of the commission in my province, or for that matter in any other province to my knowledge. But I think that in the boundaries which were established in some cases, very little consideration was given to the real problems facing people involved in the political and the electoral processes.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I could cite a number of examples in my own province where the boundaries drawn simply did not relate in any way to the natural community structures. One example is the constituency of Moose Jaw, with approximately 70,000 people, one-half of whom live in the city of Moose Jaw which is in the extreme southeast corner of the constituency which then proceeds in a westerly and north-

erly direction to within eight miles of the city of Saskatoon, goes far west to the Saskatchewan River, takes in an area west of the South Saskatchewan dam and the river in that area, which is completely cut off from the rest of the constituency.
Another example is the constituency of Meadow Lake, which comes within a few miles of the city of North Battleford and within a few miles of the city of Prince Albert. For the people living immediately adjacent to these cities, all their activities are linked to them; but for purposes of election and political activities their contact is totally with the constituency of Meadow Lake in the northwestern corner of the province.
With respect to population, terms were written into the federal legislation providing that there should not be a variation of more than 25 per cent above or below the norm for any province. But the fact was that a considerable change in population took place between 1961 and the time the redistribution was carried out. The net effect was that when the final boundaries were settled, the variation in population in constituencies in Saskatchewan was as great as it had been prior to redistribution.
I have already commented on the hearings when a number of representations were made by very interested people, and reasonable proposals were set forth. However, there was very little response from the commission, and in its official report it did not make a single change to the original proposals which had been made public. I think we should learn from this experience and consider alternatives to or changes in the legislation.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I should make it clear that I am speaking on my own behalf and not necessarily on behalf of the New Democratic Party. I think some way should be found to apply the general approach and principles involved in the legislation as originally passed, and to take into account the fact that the drawing of electoral boundaries is part of the political process. Should we not, in fact, give consideration to establishing a commission which could have as chairman a judge appointed by the Chief Justice of the province and a number of representatives appointed by the Speaker of the House of Commons as is presently the case?
Provision could also be made to include representatives from each of the recognized political parties within each province. A formula could be devised and used as a guide in deciding which political parties should have

representation on the commission and that would take account of the various points of view to be considered.
One other change which might be considered is giving the House of Commons the power to make a change in the report of a commission if the change receives approval of two-thirds or three-quarters of the members of the House.
Mr. Speaker, in my view all members of this House have a responsibility to try and make the process work as it is set out in the legislation approved some years ago. No one will argue with the fact that you cannot make everybody happy with any set of proposals. However, I do not think this should prevent members of the House doing everything that can be done with a very difficult task. I think it is very necessary that we consider this matter in that context, because we do need to take account of these problems if we are to make this process work and ensure its survival.
I hope the proposal placed before us by the hon. member for Edmonton West is either approved, or the subject matter referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speechtext:
In my constituency of Rocky Mountain we have three great national parks of Canada. They stretch from the extreme south to the extreme north of the riding and are very important to the economy of the constituency. The national parks are very important from the point of view of tourism. In addition, we have an economic community of interest throughout the riding.

Our people carry on coal mining. That activity commences in the southern portion or the riding and is carried on throughout the length of the region. We find that activity in the Crowsnest Pass area, the Canmore area, the Coal Valley area and in the Smoky River deposits which had not been developed when the commission was considering electoral boundaries in Alberta. They investigated the potential of the coal deposits in the northern part of the riding and now it is safe to say that we have a community of interest extending from the extreme south to the extreme north of the constituency.
As a result of the farsightedness the commissioners exercised, the constituency of Rocky Mountain may be the only constituency in Alberta which will not need to have its boundaries changed when constituencies are next considered for redistribution. There are at present in the constituency approximately
65,000	people. That is less than the optimum number for Alberta constituencies. But in the north end of the riding we have a rapidly growing population, and it will continue to grow for some time because of resource development taking place there.
It will not be necessary to change the constituency boundaries even after the next census has been taken. It has not, as have many other rural constituencies in western Canada, a great outflow of population which necessitates changes in boundaries; neither has it, as have many urban constituencies, a vast increase in population which requires a contraction of constituency boundaries. I suggest that the constituency of Rocky Mountain will not need to be changed when redistribution is considered again.
